newsitem.title: UK: Britain's House of Fraser to cut 1,000 jobs.
newsitem.headline: Britain's House of Fraser to cut 1,000 jobs.

text.p: The struggling British department store chain House of Fraser Plc said Monday it was cutting 1,000 jobs, or about 14 percent of its work force, and disposing of three stores in moves meant to save 10 million pounds ($16 million) a year.
The company will also clear out unwanted inventories and plans further cost-cutting steps later, it said.
Retail analysts said the company probably needed more radical surgery to improve its performance, and some were surprised Fraser did not want to sell more stores.
"I don't think this is necessarily the end of the story," said one retail analyst.
The retailer estimated the one-time costs from the moves at up to 49 million pounds ($78 million). It employed 7,000 people before the latest announcement.

Chief Executive John Coleman outlined plans in October to improve the firm's financial performance, which has been dismal since the Fayed brothers, owners of Harrods, sold stock in House of Fraser to the public in 1994.
Coleman said there were more costs to come out of the business and the firm was looking at ways to improve operating efficiencies in its stores.

"You have to say when you're trying to improve efficiency and you're looking for ways to save money there's always the likelihood or possibility of maybe further job losses," he said in a telephone interview.
Coleman said the company hoped to sell the stores -- in Eastbourne on the south coast and in Scunthorpe in northern England -- as going concerns to preserve jobs.

The three were identified as having little chance of returning to an acceptable level of profitability. Coleman said there were other problem stores in the group, but would not say which ones. Last October, House of Fraser warned it could close between five and 10 of its 51 shops.

The retailer, plagued by problems since its stock market debut, posted a loss in the first half of its current fiscal of 13.6 million pounds ($21.8 million) including special charges. Sales rose 6.1 percent, including the Christmas and January sales periods.
Coleman, brought in last April to try to revive profits, was optimistic that new merchandise due in stores later this year would help improve the group's sales performance.
He blamed a lack of focus in marketing, quality of management and stock problems for contributing to the group's troubles.
